attributes.rationale: There is no pre-machine-learning method for choosing perturbations to reach a defined cell state, so the reference is random selection from the candidate set. Among the evidence linked to this use case, only the retrospective AssayBench-Loop replay scores it, as one random draw on the same screens and budget as the other policies; the CPPC protocols measure submitted methods only, and the challenge's ranking metric only takes 0.5 as the value expected from a random ranking. NAIAD's uniform arm still ranks pairs with the model, so it is not this baseline.

attributes.question: Which genetic perturbations should I test to produce a defined cellular response?
attributes.decision: Allocate a fixed experimental budget to perturbations most likely to produce the prespecified phenotype.
inputs: A defined cell system, starting state and target phenotype
Candidate genetic perturbations and a fixed testing budget
Measured perturbations and matched controls with guide, replicate and condition metadata
The intended transfer setting: unseen genes, combinations or a new cellular context
attributes.output: A ranked experimental shortlist with predicted phenotype effects, coverage and uncertainty about unmeasured conditions.
attributes.setting: Research selection for a defined genetic-perturbation screen. Chemical interventions and combinations need their own protocols. This question concerns phenotype hits rather than expression reconstruction alone.
exclusions: Transcriptome similarity alone does not establish successful experimental selection.
Generalisation to an unseen gene, combination and cell context must be evaluated separately.
Choosing experiments to maximise information gain is a separate decision.
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Predicted cellular responses do not establish patient response or treatment-selection validity.
evidence_gaps: 61 nominations / Results 57 selected targets / README 59 targets / 50 post-QC perturbations need reconciliation; no success fraction calculated.
Automated source review only; independent human scientific review remains outstanding.
Custom ranking AUC is not ROC AUC, prospective hit rate or efficacy.
No matched-budget conventional/random prospective comparison; no antitumor efficacy, rescue or selectivity result in this endpoint.
Original model implementations/checkpoints are not pinned in the intake; no uncertainty printed.
Preprint v1; original and reimplemented ranking scores kept separate. Screen2 ranking population is enriched by original nomination methods.

Matched random comparisons are retrospective only. AssayBench-Loop replays 20 screens with one random draw and prints no uncertainty; NAIAD's uniform arm still ranks pairs with the model, so the yield of testing randomly chosen pairs is not reported.
No prospective comparison of a model shortlist against random or conventional selection at the same budget.
The retrospective comparisons (AssayBench-Loop, NAIAD) were run by the developers of one of the compared methods; no independent replication.

Retrospective hits are each screen's own significance call. In AssayBench-Loop many recovered hits are common-essential genes, and the paper does not address whether the language models saw the test screens' publications in pre-training.
Combination evidence covers four two-gene viability screens only, gives the model every single-gene effect, and counts predicted as well as measured pairs as found.

name: Evidence summary: Select perturbations for a defined cellular response
description: Plain-language summary of what the reviewed evidence shows. Draft until reviewed.

attributes.value: The evidence comes from one prospective challenge and two retrospective replays, which measure different things. In the Cancer Immunotherapy Data Science Challenge, scored prospectively in mouse T cells, the 20 original Challenge 2 submissions had a top-k overlap AUC of 0.452 to 0.566, with 17 of the 20 between 0.50 and 0.57; a random ordering is expected to score 0.5. That score is not a ROC AUC, and the genes it scores were drawn from the leading Challenge 1 nominations. In the follow-up, two nominated targets exceeded the Screen 1 targets on the immune checkpoint blockade objective; the source reports 61 nominations, 57 selected targets, 59 screen-2 genes and 50 perturbations passing quality control without reconciling them, so no success fraction follows. AssayBench-Loop replays 20 genome-wide CRISPR screens published after 2021, with each policy choosing 10 rounds of 100 genes. One random draw found 4.9% of each screen's hits on average (enrichment 1.04 over the random expectation). Language models used directly as the policy, with hit labels, reached enrichment of 1.39 to 4.81, BPMF 4.49, and the authors' handoffs from a language model to their AssayFormer up to 5.67, with the Gemini-3.1-Pro handoff finding 27.7% of hits. Many recovered hits are common-essential genes: 30.1% for that handoff, 18.6% for the random draw and 99.1% for a baseline that picks earlier screens' hits. Test screens were kept only if the best language model already passed a performance floor on them, and the paper does not say whether the models saw the screens' publications in training. The authors ran every row, and no uncertainty is printed. For two-gene combinations, NAIAD's replay of four viability screens counted how many of each screen's 200 strongest pairs the model ranked in its top 200 after four rounds: 143.0, 141.7, 99.7 and 150.0 when it acquired the pairs with the largest predicted effect, against 93.3, 70.3, 38.7 and 81.3 when it acquired pairs uniformly at random (means of three replicates). That count includes pairs the model predicted but never measured, and the uniform arm still uses the model's ranking, so it is not the yield of testing random pairs. The challenge's submissions scored close to a random ordering, while in both replays the leading model-guided policies scored above the random or uniform arm; the two differ in endpoint, candidate set, setting and who ran them, so their results cannot be compared directly. No source compares a model shortlist with random selection prospectively at the same budget.
